## Sticki Rolls is Turning Stickers into the New Social Currency

Listen to this article· 7:23

Of the many hobbies that emerged over the last century, sticker collecting has managed to adapt, evolve, and maintain cultural relevance. Even in our current era of digital connectivity, Gen Alpha is collecting stickers as a form of self-expression and cultural currency.

Sticki Rolls has undoubtedly helped drive this analog hobby resurgence. The brand has gone viral many times for its “satisfyingly stretchy” collectibles and niche sticker bundles. And its power extends far beyond novelty. It sits at the intersection of beauty, collectibles, and the creator economy.

“The innovation pipeline within Sticki Rolls is totally fashion-driven, from pendants to sticker books, all the different ways you can collect, show off your collection, and share with your friends,” said Michelle Wong, SVP of Global Marketing for Jazwares, the distributor and brand-development partner behind Sticki Rolls’ global expansion. “What’s really unique about this moment in time is [fashion] is really centered around joy, and it’s a demonstration of the things that make you happy. Even at the Gen Alpha stage of life, it’s such a critical part of every day and growing up, so we love being part of that moment. It’s an incredible place to be with a product.”

Its emphasis on joy, maximalism, and self-expression has quickly made Sticki Rolls an online juggernaut. Founders Josh Loerzel and Lev Nelson prioritized organic growth on YouTube and launched the brand account during the 2024 unboxing and “haul” culture wave. Since then, the brand has surpassed 1B views and 1.9M subscribers.

Sticki Rolls has acquired an incredibly loyal fan base, largely due to its close ties with creators like Anna Altamirano and Erin Degan, the Kawaii artists who drove the original Sticki Rolls collection. But its August 2026 pop-up at the Chillhouse store in Soho showed the power of bringing Sticki Rolls’ tactile product offering into the physical world.

Over two days, the Sticki Rolls x Chillhouse pop-up experience hosted nearly 1,000 guests, 500 of whom opted in for complimentary sticker manicures. The event served as a product preview of sorts, giving guests a sneak peek at Sticki Mates, a new collectible bag-charm collection that adds to the brand’s signature assortment of sticker bracelets. But the event also validated how Sticki Rolls could move beyond wholesale presence and into an immersive, fully branded brick-and-mortar experience.

> “The thought behind this experience was: how do we harness all this energy and bring it into a real-life environment? How do we create an experience where fans can actually live and experience it together, and actually have a physical touchstone to the brand itself?”
> 
> ‍_- Michelle Wong, SVP of Global Marketing, Jazzwares
> 
> ‍_

Because of the brand’s roots online, the pop-up had a powerful digital halo effect. Google search interest rose 50% week over week and 130% month over month immediately after the event. The Sticki Rolls YouTube account also acquired more than 20,000 new subscribers since the event.

![Image 3](https://cdn.futurecommerce.com/5d7da04028ecca2357d6b3b0/6a92085424938988df844bf7_CNC_StickiRolls_Press3.jpg)

### ‍

The Strategy in Motion: A Product Experience Rooted in ‘Girlhood’

Sticki Rolls has achieved cultural relevance because the product experience is inherently cultural. “Sticki Rolls is an incredibly special brand and product because how you interact with the product—its shareability and collectability—engenders friendship and connection,” Wong said. “I’ve always looked at Sticki Rolls as this definitive product within girlhood.”

It makes sense, then, to create a space that evokes the same feeling and experience, where digital and physical could coexist, and where young shoppers could authentically express themselves while forming new friendships in the store and even online after their visit.

"There’s so much about the digital experience that is innate in this generation, so it’s not either/or—it’s more about how do we ensure that all of those ways to interact with a brand are present and we get to take that into real life,” Wong said. “Sticki Rolls allows their fans, their consumers, to have that in-real-life human connection. The sharing, the collecting that’s happening in playgrounds and parties and schools, actually fosters a really sweet human interaction."

Chillhouse represented an ideal complementary brand, known for its trendy nail art and press-ons, but also its aspirational aesthetic. Making manicures part of the “Sticki Rolls experience” turned what most girls consider a rite of passage into a product-trial experience. Wong noted that when the team considered how a sticker brand could and should show up, fashion and beauty “squarely fit within where the brand also inhabits.”

> “The nail salon felt like a natural way to show up, but also a little unexpected. That’s where a lot of the joy gets sparked, just fueling that fandom.”_- Michelle Wong, Jazzwares_

The Sticki Rolls-inspired manicures, paired with BFF bracelet-making, a meet-and-greet with the brand’s two most popular creator partners (Anna and Erin), and a branded “Sticki Café,” turned a product reveal into a community-driven experience engineered for Gen Alpha and their parents, which reflects the very real media consumption habits of most households today.

"The primary audience is certainly Gen Alpha, but we are experiencing media very differently today than when I was growing up,” Wong said. “It’s very much a shared household experience and, at the end of the day, it’s jewelry. It’s a great way for families to feel connected—you could have a mommy-and-me moment. There’s absolutely a halo of who else gets to really enjoy this content and experience."

![Image 4](https://cdn.futurecommerce.com/5d7da04028ecca2357d6b3b0/6a9208968314e4ad9126bafe_CNC_StickiRolls_Press11.jpg)

### Vision: A Dopamine Roadshow

The final pop-up design was unmistakably Sticki Rolls, from the sticker art on the walls to the character pillows and pops of pink throughout the space. “We thought through every detail to make sure that when people show up, it’s undeniably Sticki Rolls,” Wong said. “That joy and connection is immediately communicated as soon as you step into the space.”

The end experience undeniably resonated, given the long-tail value Sticki Rolls saw in the form of pop-up visits, Google searches, and social-media follows. While KPIs put a number to the investment, Wong noted they’d pay just as much attention to the comments because that is where new opportunities lie.

“We know this audience is already incredibly vocal, active, and highly engaged on social,” Wong said. “We want to see a lot of that, either covered by the fans that are there, or comments that say they want us to come to their city. We want to watch that engine start really rolling and use that data to inform what is next. What are the things that really got people excited, and where we go next.”

Wong didn’t give a firm answer about what’s next, but she jokingly remarked that they could easily bring the pop-up on the road. “Let’s do a tour or roadshow,” she said. “There are so many fans, and there’s so much energy for Sticki Rolls. Title: SKIMS Marketing Strategy: Kim Kardashian’s Billion-Dollar Brand

URL Source: https://www.marketergems.com/p/skims-marketing-strategy-kim-kardashian

Published Time: 2026-09-03T11:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Howdy, Marketer!

If you ask the average consumer why SKIMS is worth billions, they will give you a one-word answer: **Kim**.

They assume it is just another celebrity cash-grab where a famous founder slaps her name on cheap white-label inventory, pushes a few Instagram posts, and watches the wire transfers roll in.

But if celebrity status alone guaranteed a multi-billion-dollar D2C empire, every A-lister with 50 million followers would be running a unicorn.

**Celebrity brands often fail within 3 years** because they treat their audience as a monetization target rather than a community, relying on vanity metrics over product utility.

SKIMS succeeded because they identified a massive structural hole in an sleepy, outdated category - **shapewear** - and reframed it entirely.

They turned solutionwear into outer-wear, body compression into body celebration, and functional undergarments into high-fashion status symbols.

[![Image 1](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/d0338fa2-596a-41e3-ba33-630fbb0a55b1/id-TJMtrvX_1788362672014.png?t=1788362682)](https://skims.com/?utm_campaign=skims-marketing-strategy-kim-kardashian-s-billion-dollar-brand&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com)

## Today's Treasure Trove

##### advertisement

## Empanada | Drive B2B Pipeline By Activating Your Team On LinkedIn

[![Image 2](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/af423819-0aa0-4c89-8dc5-0e2db90d43a6/watch-the-loom.png?t=1787784657)](https://www.empanada.social/?utm_campaign=skims-marketing-strategy-kim-kardashian-s-billion-dollar-brand&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com#video)

Your people are a **huge, untapped lead channel**.

Empanada solves that.

I put together a 4-minute video showing exactly how this works.

If it looks like something your team could use, hit reply and I'll get you set up.

## What Is SKIMS

**Some Stats:**

SKIMS is a shapewear, underwear, and loungewear brand founded by Kim Kardashian in September 2019, built around inclusive sizing and a "[solutions for every body](https://skims.com/?utm_campaign=skims-marketing-strategy-kim-kardashian-s-billion-dollar-brand&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com)" positioning instead of the old Victoria's Secret angel aesthetic.

## Target Demographics and Positioning

SKIMS has 2 major target demographics:

*   **Primary Demographic:**

Gen Z and Millennial women aged 18 to 34 who prioritize both comfort and aesthetics drive about [70%](https://businessmodelcanvastemplate.com/blogs/target-market/skims-target-market?utm_campaign=skims-marketing-strategy-kim-kardashian-s-billion-dollar-brand&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com) of revenue. They are digital natives consumed by social video, heavily influenced by pop culture trends, and actively seeking body-positive apparel.

*   **Emerging Demographic:**

Men aged 18 to 45, targeted through the launch of SKIMS Mens, backed by high-profile athletic partnerships with leagues like the [NBA](https://skims.com/en-in/pages/nba?utm_campaign=skims-marketing-strategy-kim-kardashian-s-billion-dollar-brand&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com).

### Positioning

For decades, **the shapewear market operated on shame**. The underlying consumer promise was simple: _buy this product so nobody notices your body's perceived flaws._

The packaging was sterile, the colors were limited to standard black and pale nude, and the retail buying experience was hidden away in dusty department store corners.

SKIMS executed a **textbook positioning pivo**t.

Instead of marketing shapewear as a hidden fix, they repositioned it as a foundation piece meant to be seen.

First, they engineered inclusivity into the physical product rather than making it an afterthought marketing campaign.

Launching with **9 distinct nude shades** across a size spectrum of XXS to 5X, SKIMS ensured that "nude" was no longer synonymous with fair skin.

![Image 3](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/3bdb26c9-8c3a-4a89-a745-1a452d20cf61/image.jpeg?t=1788362814)

Second, SKIMS shifted the category from _utility_ to _lifestyle_.

The garments are designed with smooth, seam-free silhouettes that encourage wearers to style them as standalone tops, bodysuits, and outerwear. This helps to increase usage frequency and customer lifetime value (LTV).

❝

### 1. Kim's following is owned infrastructure

Brands have to pay influencers for reach.

SKIMS skipped that step entirely because **the founder is the influencer**.

Kim Kardashian is the distribution channel, with [344 million](https://www.instagram.com/kimkardashian/?utm_campaign=skims-marketing-strategy-kim-kardashian-s-billion-dollar-brand&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com) followers on Instagram, more reach than Victoria's Secret ever had with their Fashion Show at its peak.

**Every launch gets amplified for free**, at a scale that would cost a competitor tens of millions in media spend.

### 2. Artificial Scarcity & The "Drop" Infrastructure

Borrowing heavily from streetwear playbook pioneers like Supreme and Yeezy, **SKIMS operates on a tight drop schedule**.

Instead of keeping a massive, static inventory live on their site year-round, they release limited-edition colorways, seasonal fabrics, and high-profile collaborations in batch drops.

This creates three critical operational advantages:

*   **Urgency & Conversion:**

Customers know that if they do not buy a new shade of the _Fits Everybody Bodysuit_ within 15 minutes of launch, it will sell out and hit eBay at a 200% markup. This eliminates purchase hesitation.

*   **Zero-Cost Retention:**

Every product drop serves as a high-intent reason to send an email or SMS notification, eliminating the need to offer constant price discounts to drive repeat purchases.

*   **Predictable Cash Flow:**

Pre-announcing drops allows SKIMS to gauge demand via waitlists, optimizing production runs and drastically reducing overstock risks.

### 3. Culture-jacking through category-defying partnerships

SKIMS has partnered with the NBA, WNBA, USA Basketball, Nike, Fendi, Swarovski, Dolce & Gabbana, and The North Face.

That's a deliberate strategy to borrow credibility and audiences from categories **where SKIMS has no natural right to exist**.

Take the WNBA deal: tied to the start of the WNBA season, SKIMS launched this campaign:

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kasOxWqow9o)

That's a shapewear brand embedding itself into live sports broadcasts, a channel it has zero organic reach in on its own.

The market moved on a shapewear-brand collaboration announcement. That's the clearest signal you'll get that "SKIMS" has become shorthand for cultural relevance and reach.

The partnership also lets Nike tap into SKIMS' extensive reach to introduce female athletes to a broader audience, right as women's sports viewership was exploding.

**SKIMS essentially became the bridge brand** connecting a hot cultural moment (rising women's sports fandom) to a legacy sportswear giant that needed a faster way in.

### 4. Strategic Influencer Seeding and Organic UGC

While SKIMS spends heavily on high-concept paid media, their real growth engine is **grassroots micro-influencer seeding**.

Before any major collection drops, thousands of unboxing packages are sent to creators across TikTok and Instagram.

Crucially, SKIMS does not restrict seeding to ultra-famous fashion influencers.

**They seed across diverse body types, skin tones, and age brackets**.

This creates a cascade of user-generated content (UGC) showing the real-world compression, stretch, and lift of the products without professional studio lighting or Photoshop.

When a consumer sees ten different women of varying body shapes post unedited videos showing how a SKIMS dress fits, trust is established far faster than any polished 30-second commercial could achieve.

### 5. Owned channels do the unglamorous heavy lifting.

Behind all the culture-jacking, there's a boring, disciplined engine running underneath. **SKIMS sends about five emails a week** to its list announcing new product drops, restocks of popular products, retail collaborations, and direct calls to purchase.

![Image 4](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/c127e1dc-8799-4503-b443-2939cd988cc8/image.png?t=1788362814)

That's just relentless owned-channel cadence, doing what paid social increasingly can't: cheap, direct, repeatable reach into an audience that already opted in.

❝

## Wrap Up

The SKIMS story isn't really about celebrity power, even though that's the headline everyone reaches for.

It's about **category redefinition**.

It’s what happens when you pair genuine product-market fit (solving for real bodies, real skin tones, real comfort) with an owned distribution channel, and then you layer disciplined scarcity and constant cultural borrowing on top of it.

Kim Kardashian built SKIMS by understanding supply chains, retention math, and the difference between hype and loyalty.

✌️,

Tom from Marketer Gems

Title: TikTok comments are getting more interactive with voice comments, polls, and more

URL Source: https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/03/tiktok-comments-are-getting-more-interactive-with-voice-comments-polls-and-more/

Published Time: 2026-09-03T13:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
TikTok’s comment sections are getting an upgrade. The social network announced on Thursday that it’s rolling out new features for its comment sections, including voice comments, comment polls, photo carousel comments, and Live Photo comments.

With the additions, the app is borrowing features from messaging apps as it looks to deepen engagement on its platform. By bundling voice, polls, and photo comments, the company aims to make comment sections places where people linger and interact with each other, rather than simply leave feedback underneath a video.

“Sound and music have shaped TikTok from the very beginning, turning songs into trends and audio clips into jokes shared across the app,” TikTok wrote in a [blog post](https://newsroom.tiktok.com/say-more-in-the-comments?lang=en). “Now, we’re bringing that same energy to the comment section with Voice Comments, a new way to post and listen to audio messages directly under any video.”

![Image 1](https://techcrunch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tiktok-voice-comments.png?w=680)

**Image Credits:**TikTok

To leave a voice comment, users need to tap the microphone icon in the comment box and record a message up to a minute long. Once the voice comment is posted, anyone can tap to listen.

A TikTok spokesperson told TechCrunch that voice comments are subject to the same Community Guidelines as other content on the platform. The company uses a combination of human and automated detection tools, including speech-to-text transcription, to identify and remove content that violates its policies.

Voice comments are rolling out globally over the next month to users 18 and older.

Additionally, creators can now add a poll when commenting on their own videos, a feature that had been previously available to some, but is now available globally.

TikTok says the polls can be used for things like voting on the next video idea, picking an outfit, deciding what to cook, and more. Creators can choose up to five options for viewers to vote on and then set a time frame for the poll. As votes come in, creators can follow results directly in the comment section.

![Image 2](https://techcrunch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tiktok-polls.png?w=680)

**Image Credits:**TikTok

With photo carousel comments, people can now add up to nine photos in a single comment, after previously only being able to add one at a time. Plus, users can now upload Live Photo comments, which TikTok says will allow for “a brief burst of motion” that allows others to see a quick preview of the moment before viewing the full image.

Live Photo comments are now available globally, while photo carousel comments are rolling out globally over the next month.

I see a lot of SEO proposals and reports; most SEO firms are not being truthful to their clients. It’s 2026, and an agency is definitely not needed for the same reason it was in 2022 before ChatGPT popped onto the scene.

_**[Sponsored by [Semrush](https://ai-visibility-index.semrush.com/downloads/chatgpt-vs-ai-mode?utm\_source=newsletter&utm\_medium=influencers&utm\_campaign=socialorganic\_partners\_futureofseo&utm\_term=social\_organic&utm\_content=elischwartz\_september03)]**_

Discover the differences in the brands being mentioned, the sources being cited, and the competitive sets they create across 22 industries.**_

_**[Download for free](https://ai-visibility-index.semrush.com/downloads/chatgpt-vs-ai-mode?utm\_source=newsletter&utm\_medium=influencers&utm\_campaign=socialorganic\_partners\_futureofseo&utm\_term=social\_organic&utm\_content=elischwartz\_september03)**_

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WszP!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb8577ccc-56bc-4f2c-a274-48edc69d8310_1632x810.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WszP!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb8577ccc-56bc-4f2c-a274-48edc69d8310_1632x810.png)

The pre-AI-era agency was driven by a content model that drove the entire agency industry: a team of freelance or full-time employed writers churning out 500-word posts targeting long-tail keywords. The bulk of the agency margin was driven by this model because the agency could tack on 50%-100% on what the actual content cost them to produce. To adapt to AI, many of these same agencies have done nothing more than rename their content teams “AEO specialists.” These new experts do the same work as before, but they just swapped the word “keyword” for “prompt” because the client is not sophisticated enough to notice.

The truth is, if an LLM can write that article faster and cheaper than the agency writer, why do SEO agencies still exist? The answer is that it shouldn’t if this is all the agency does. This isn’t a new reality; rather, AI just made it impossible to hide.

**Content alone is not SEO**

When it came to SEO, content was never the value an agency provided. In-house teams could also hire freelance writers and manage them. What the client really wanted to pay for was [growth](https://www.productledseo.com/p/what-is-the-success-metric-and-kpi). The agency sold the monthly packaging, claiming that their agency process led to growth. Agencies delivered content because it was easy to scope and easy to hand over as a deliverable. Twenty articles a month, briefed, written, and delivered, is a lot easier to scope than the ambiguous “growth.” Some agencies sold guest posts for [links,](https://www.productledseo.com/p/are-you-neglecting-your-internal) which is also just content, but on someone else’s site. This was just as easy to scope and deliver.

(I have already discussed technical SEO as an AEO deliverable in this [post.](https://www.productledseo.com/p/the-role-of-technical-seo-in-aeo))

For the growth KPI, they created and pointed to rankings dashboards. This appeared to be progress because it was measurable, and agencies kept their jobs when the dashboard was green. When the dashboard turned red, the agency was replaced with another that could deliver green dashboards. In reality, [strategy](https://www.productledseo.com/p/how-to-build-an-seo-roadmap) was supposed to be the real value beneath it all, but agencies never had to prove that because the content itself was the deliverable everyone could see and count.

With the introduction of AI, the primary deliverable of content is worthless. Anyone with Claude access can produce better, meatier mediocre articles nearly autonomously than a typical agency team can ship in a quarter. This is why there are so many social media posts about firing agencies and replacing them with Claude. The core agency deliverable of dashboards and content can truly be replicated by a $20 Claude subscription.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XOhz!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F440b88b2-e12a-498d-bb59-b5e68d733b51_2124x884.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XOhz!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F440b88b2-e12a-498d-bb59-b5e68d733b51_2124x884.png)

To combat this client churn, now is the moment for agencies to pivot their offering and for clients to demand something new. For the agency model to survive, agencies should stop selling content immediately. A business paying an agency in 2026 purely to churn out blog posts is paying for something with less differentiated value than an LLM subscription. There is plenty of real work left that AI can’t touch, and given how many companies are distracted by AI FOMO, the right work is more valuable now than it’s ever been.

**Strategy as THE deliverable**

Strategy is the primary asset agencies should be selling. Real strategy means understanding why a business, with its ICP, should own visibility in problems its competitors haven’t yet figured out. This requires a deep understanding of the customer, the product, and the[jobs-to-be-done](https://www.productledseo.com/p/seo-and-aeo-jobs-to-be-done). Doing this is hard work the internal team might not be able to execute on its own, which is why an agency should be brought in to do that heavy lifting.

An organization’s internal team might have customer support data, product feedback, and brand research, but they don’t know how to turn it into a compelling strategy they can execute to drive growth. The lazy way out of just using a keyword tool is the wrong approach. The same internal team can also purchase a keyword tool and make color-coded keyword plans.

They need an agency to do what they can’t do on their own and, most importantly, to turn it into meaningful growth. Companies can certainly bring these tasks and skills in-house, but there are many inherent benefits to using an agency, including instant access to talent (assuming the agency has it), flexibility, and scalability. Additionally, agencies working across multiple accounts will have insights that no single team or employee could access if they focus on only one company. Ultimately, the best option for many organizations might be to in-house these functions, but that is not an option for many.

**PR as an agency effort**

PR is the second focus area where agencies can help, and most SEO agencies have never done this. They bought links and guest posts, but didn’t deliver meaningful PR work, because that is hard. More than ever, PR is important because it will shape the brand perception reflected in LLMs as citations. An answer engine builds its response from sources with a track record of being cited elsewhere, so the same signal that earns a journalist's trust ultimately feeds an LLM

Getting mentioned in the answer an LLM gives someone requires the same thing as getting mentioned in the New York Times: a third party with credibility decided your brand was worth citing. You can’t fake your way into that with better technical SEO or an audit.

This is earned by being the source a journalist trusts, the founder who says something worth quoting, or the company whose data a researcher cites because it’s actually useful. SEO agencies spent years producing fake outcomes. I have seen past clients pay their way into the NY Times, but it was in places that never mattered for SEO and certainly not for AEO. Fake efforts no longer work when the goal is revenue. A guest post on a page no one, not a crawler or human, will ever see does not move any needles.

**The agency of the future**

To construct this sort of agency, it will look completely different. There are no writers on staff, or if there are, they’re doing original reporting and customer research, not grinding out keyword-stuffed posts that no one will ever read. This agency's output is not measured by articles written or links acquired; the actual deliverables are strategies, execution plans, and performance feedback. This agency conducts research and provides answers on how to win in ways the client could not achieve on their own.

The value of this agency is measured by its relationships with journalists and analysts, the way a PR firm would, except now that relationship directly determines whether an AI model treats the brand as a trustworthy source on a given topic. The agency coaches the client’s actual subject matter experts on what to say publicly, because those experts talking in their own voice on a podcast is worth more to visibility now than a hundred blog posts ever were.

The agency of the future is much smaller than the one it replaced, and it bills more like a strategic consultancy than one measured by words written or minutes in a meeting. Most agencies will run from this model because it's harder to scale and doesn't fit the model of driving margin with cheap labor.

These agencies will have to be truly creative and more agile than their clients to justify not being fired when clients in-source their basic deliverables or simply use a Claude subscription. The agencies that remain profitable in two years will be the ones that have figured out how to layer PR outcomes onto SEO logic and provide strategies that work in real life, not just in a slide deck.

Yes, agencies should exist, but the best ones will look nothing like today’s agencies. As always, reach out if you want recommendations.

Title: Research: What Drives Gen Z Brand Loyalty in 2026?

URL Source: https://www.rivaltech.com/blog/research-gen-z-loyalty-2026

Published Time: 2026-08-31T19:17:06.000Z

Markdown Content:
![Image 1: A survey of 903 Gen Z consumers in the US and Canada reveals what drives Gen Z brand loyalty](https://www.rivaltech.com/hubfs/Gen%20Z%20loyalty%20study%202026%20-%20images.jpg)

The good news? Gen Z can be loyal to brands. But you have to earn it. Here's how.

KC

[Kelvin Claveria](https://www.rivaltech.com/blog/author/kelvin-claveria)Kelvin Claveria is Senior Director of Demand Generation and Content Marketing at Rival Technologies and Reach3 Insights | 31 Aug 2026

Marketers have spent years being told that Gen Z is impossible to hold onto. That they're fickle, brand-agnostic, and ready to bail the moment something cheaper or newer shows up.

It's a tidy story. New research from our team at Rival Technologies also shows that it's also mostly wrong.

Using our [conversational market research platform](https://www.rivaltech.com/platform), we surveyed 903 Gen Z consumers across Canada and the US in July and August 2026 to understand how this generation actually thinks about brands. The picture is more interesting and nuanced.

In this article, we share some of our key findings. You can also [check out the full report](https://www.rivaltech.com/gen-z-brand-loyalty) to learn more.

First, the myth: Gen Z can absolutely be loyal

Here's the good news for us marketers: Gen Z brand loyalty is not dead.

When we asked Gen Z how often they stick with a brand they like instead of switching to a cheaper or newer option, 64% said they stay loyal "always" or "most of the time." Only a small fraction said they rarely or never stick around.

So despite all the options available to Gen Z, the capacity for loyalty is clearly there. This raises an important question: why are brands having a hard time earning the loyalty of this generation?

## The single biggest driver of Gen Z brand loyalty

Do you really get your Gen Z customers?

Based on our research, the answer is most likely not. Only 11% of Gen Z say brands understand them "really well." That's a sad number, but looking deeper provides a glimpse of hope. Among Gen Z who feel a brand gets them "really well," 45% are loyal "always." Among those who feel brands miss the mark, just 5% are.

That's roughly a nine-times difference. Feeling understood is the strongest signal of loyalty we found, stronger than any single product feature or perk.

A word of caution on that number: it's based on a smaller subgroup (the 11% who feel truly understood), so treat the exact ratio as directional rather than precise. It also shows an association, not proof of cause.Still, the direction is unmistakable. Loyalty isn't won by shouting louder. It's won by making people feel like you actually get them.

## What actually earns Gen Z brand loyalty

One stereotype about Gen Z is that they pick brands that have values that align with theirs. Previous research has shows, for instance, that Gen Z care about [social activism](https://www.reach3insights.com/more-than-just-tok) or sustainability.

Our research shows that this might be shifting a bit. Perhaps due to inflation or the job market, but it seems like what Gen Z is looking for these days are a bit more practical.

When we asked Gen Z directly what keeps them coming back to a brand, the answers were refreshingly unglamorous. The fundamentals dominate:

*   **Price and value — 82%**
*   **Product quality — 80%**
*   Rewards or perks — 41%
*   Alignment with my values — 36%
*   Customer service — 33%
*   Recommendation from friends or family — 28%
*   Recommendation from influencers — 9%

Price, value, and quality tower over everything else. The more fashionable loyalty levers—purpose, values-alignment, and influencer endorsements—trail far behind. Values-alignment matters to about a third of Gen Z, but as a tiebreaker on top of a good product, not a substitute for one.

And influencer marketing, which takes [up to 25% of marketing budgets](https://www.storyboard18.com/influencer-marketing/d2c-brands-put-10-25-of-marketing-budgets-into-creators-agencies-see-40-50-of-digital-spend-109298.htm) now, ranked dead last with only 9% of Gen Z saying it influences their loyalty.

This need for practicality is reflected how Gen Z describe the brands they're loyal to. One example:

> "Adidas always has strong sales. It's a brand of great quality. Their rewards program is better than their competitors." — He/him, US, 25–29

Another example:

> "I recommend Anker because it's reliable, never breaks, charges fast, and they actually honor warranties." — He/him, US, 25–29

Even the values-driven answers are anchored to a product that delivers first:

> "I'm loyal to DUER for pants. They're uniquely made, look professional, and are as comfortable as sweatpants. The company cares about sustainability, is Canadian-founded, and offers great value." — He/him, Canada, 25–29

Values are a multiplier on a good product, never a rescue for a mediocre one.

Of course, this might change as macroeconomic forces evolve or as Gen Z move to a different lifestage. It's a reminder that companies need to engage Gen Z continuously (through [insight communities](https://www.rivaltech.com/why-insight-communities) and other similar programs) to understand where they are today and how their attitudes and behaviors may change in the future.

## Gen Z loyalty is not one-size-fits-all

If your company is building your Gen Z marketing strategy now, our research suggests that you need to be more specific in your targeting. Different Gen Z groups have different needs and expectations.

### **US vs Canada Gen Z markets**

Interestingly, our research shows that American Gen Z are nearly three times more likely than Canadians to say brands get them "really well" (17% versus 6%), and about twice as likely to be unconditionally loyal.

Canadian Gen Z are more skeptical and harder to win. The same campaign will tend to land warmer in the US and flatter in Canada, so a credibility-first, prove-it approach works better north of the border.

A single North American Gen Z marketing is unlikely to do well given these differences in perspectives.

### **Gen Z loyalty drivers shift with age**

The youngest cohort (18–20) leans more on discovery and peer influence, while older Gen Z (25–29) increasingly rewards reliability and service. Customer service climbs steadily as a loyalty driver with age, from 22% among the youngest to 38% among the oldest.

These findings are a reminder that "Gen Z" is not a monolithic group. Really there are [3 Gen Z age groups to consider](https://www.rivaltech.com/blog/next-generation-of-consumers). In this case, age is not just a number — it's a reflection of their lifestage and their different needs. A teenager living at home has a very different need from a mid-20-something moving in with a partner for the first time.

## Recommendation for marketers

Hopefully our research shows that Gen Z loyalty isn't a mystery, and it isn't out of reach. But brands need to earn that loyalty. Here are three key recommendations from our research:

Get the fundamentals right first. Price, value, and quality are the price of entry. No amount of purpose messaging compensates for a product that doesn't deliver.

Make them feel understood. This is the real differentiator and the strongest predictor of loyalty. Invest in relevance and personalization. Make sure you're using real Gen Z customer insights to inform your strategy.

Use values as a multiplier, not a lead. Values-alignment deepens loyalty for a meaningful slice of Gen Z, but only when the product already earns their trust.

The generation everyone calls disloyal is, in fact, ready to commit. Most brands just haven't given them a reason.

Overall, our study reiterates that to earn the heart and minds of Gen Z, brands must invest in getting to know these young consumers deeply. Whether it's through [insight communities](https://www.rivaltech.com/why-insight-communities), a syndicated program like [Rival's Emerging Consumer Index](https://www.rivaltech.com/emerging-consumer-index-request), or doing custom studies with [top Gen Z market research companies](https://www.rivaltech.com/blog/top-gen-z-market-research-companies), the brands that prove to young consumers that they really get them will win.

[![Image 2: Kelvin Claveria](https://www.rivaltech.com/hubfs/Kelvin%20-%20square.jpeg)](https://www.rivaltech.com/blog/author/kelvin-claveria)

Written by[Kelvin Claveria](https://www.rivaltech.com/blog/author/kelvin-claveria)Kelvin Claveria is Senior Director of Demand Generation and Content Marketing at Rival Technologies and Reach3 Insights

Title: How to Handle Negative Comments on Reddit - Standing on Giants

URL Source: https://www.standingongiants.com/blog/how-to-handle-negative-comments-on-reddit/

Markdown Content:
Search almost any big consumer brand on Reddit and sort by relevance. You will often find something like this.

A thread asking whether the company is a scam. A post titled “[Brand] nightmare”. A comment recommending “anything except them”, with a few hundred upvotes agreeing.

That page is now doing real work. It ranks in Google, it gets cited by AI assistants when someone asks whether your product is any good, and it is usually the first honest-looking thing a prospective customer reads about you.

This is easily the most common reason brands tell us they cannot go near Reddit. The criticism is too loud, too visible and too permanent.

Engaging feels like walking into a room where everyone is already talking about you.

But that room exists whether you walk into it or not.

How should a brand handle negative comments on Reddit?

## The short answer

Do not try to remove, or suppress them.

Engage a small number of them well, as a named human, with disclosure, in the threads where you can add something nobody else can. Leave the rest alone.

Negative sentiment is not the problem to solve. Unanswered negative sentiment is.

Read the longer version below…

![Image 1](https://www.standingongiants.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/andre-hunter-5otlbgWJlLs-unsplash-scaled.jpg)

## **Why negative Reddit threads matter more than they used to**

Two things have changed.

First, Reddit’s visibility in search has climbed steeply, and LLMs lean on it heavily when answering questions about brands. That is precisely because it reads as unfiltered peer opinion, and upvote weight is one of the strongest signals for what gets surfaced and cited.

Second, and more usefully, engagement patterns are shifting.

In a recent client listening report covering several hundred threads, we found positive threads drawing almost exactly the same upvote weight as negative ones. That is unusual for Reddit, where negativity has historically travelled much further.

Negative threads still generated longer comment trails, because criticism invites debate and praise invites agreement. But the reach was level.

The implication is significant. A well-pitched, genuinely helpful contribution can now expect comparable visibility to a complaint.

You are not shouting into a headwind. Your Reddit footprint is not fixed, and a more balanced footprint produces a more balanced answer when someone asks an AI about you.

## **Stop thinking about moderation. Start thinking about community management.**

Most brands approach negativity with a moderation mindset. What can we get taken down, hidden, or switched off?

On Reddit, that instinct is not just wrong, it is unavailable.

You do not (usually) moderate the subreddit. Volunteer moderators do, and they have often cared for that space for years. Asking them to remove criticism of you is the fastest way to burn the one relationship that matters most.

Even in communities you do own, suppression is a poor tool. It teaches members that the space is not safe to be honest in, and pushes the conversation somewhere you cannot see it.

Community management does something different. It redirects behaviour, educates members and shepherds conduct rather than policing it.

You are not trying to eliminate negative posts. You are trying to change what happens next in the thread.

Four principles sit underneath that.

Show Work  Be open. Explain your decisions and your reasons in detail. Treat members as intelligent adults and they will generally behave like them. Reddit has an unusually low tolerance for vagueness and an unusually high one for detail.

Praise Often  Be relentlessly positive. Reinforce the behaviour you want rather than punishing the behaviour you do not. Thanking someone for a well-argued complaint does more for the tone of a subreddit than correcting the person shouting.

Teach First  Educate before you moderate. Most “bad” behaviour is unfamiliarity with the norms rather than malice. Teach, do not discipline.

Stay Firm  Be conversational and assertive, never loud. You can hold a position firmly without shouting or bullying. Corporate defensiveness and aggression fail in the same way: both signal that you are protecting the brand rather than helping the person.

As Keith Nieves, who runs [Sonos’s Reddit presence as KeithFromSonos](https://www.standingongiants.com/blog/reddit-case-study-sonos/), puts it: “Don’t act in service of the brand, be in service of the community member.”

He built that credibility long before the app crisis hit, which is exactly why it held during it.

## **The grey area: frustration, or a genuine problem?**

Some negativity is straightforward. Someone has had a bad experience, they vent, you help or you listen, and they move on.

The harder cases are the ones that do not break any rules but still drag the space down. The member who shows up every few weeks with the same complaint. The commenter whose criticism has quietly turned personal.

Not quite a violation, but not nothing either.

At Standing on Giants we use the **REACT framework** for these judgement calls. It works whether you are managing your own community or engaging as a guest on Reddit.

**R, Review the user’s history.** Are they always negative, or occasionally frustrated? Have they added value before? Look at tone, timing and patterns. One rough day does not mean bad intentions, though repeated friction might.

**E, Evaluate the nature of their comments.** Is the criticism fair, or has it gone personal? Look for language designed to provoke or undermine rather than to be heard. If a comment crosses the line, escalate internally.

**A, Assess willingness to accept support.** Frustrated members usually engage when help is offered, even a little. People acting in bad faith tend to ignore support, reject it, or vanish until the next flare-up. No engagement is a red flag.

**C, Consider the time frame.** Someone venting once every few months may just need space. The same complaints resurfacing repeatedly despite past help points to something deeper. Frequency and predictability matter.

**T, Take thoughtful action.** If the person seems open, or the issue looks isolated, keep the door open. If the pattern continues, start documenting it. Eventually that may mean a Do Not Engage list, and a decision to protect the wider community instead.

And when you are on the fence, ask your team. A second opinion is the cheapest safeguard you have.

## What good looks like

You will not measure this in sentiment score movements next month. Reddit is closer to an insurance policy than a campaign. You build the relationship before you need it, and the return shows up when something goes wrong.

Realistic markers of progress:

*   Recurring myths get corrected faster, and stay corrected
*   The high-ranking threads about you contain more accurate information
*   Your brand appears in search and AI summaries with fewer factual errors
*   Moderator relationships are healthy enough that you can pick up the phone
*   Sentiment trends improve gradually, without you having removed a single post

![Image 2](https://www.standingongiants.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/hannah-busing-Zyx1bK9mqmA-unsplash-1-scaled.jpg)

## The takeaway

The goal was never to shut down criticism. It is to keep the space safe for constructive conversation, including constructive criticism of you.

Not every negative comment is a crisis. Not every difficult member is a troll.

And a subreddit full of complaints is not a reason to stay away. It is evidence that people care enough about your product to argue about it.

With a clear process, real context and a team behind you, you will know when to show patience and when to draw the line.

![Image 3](https://www.standingongiants.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/helena-lopes-PGnqT0rXWLs-unsplash-scaled.jpg)

## Ready to figure out Reddit?

If negative threads are already shaping how customers see your brand, you need a plan rather than a takedown request. Book a free Reddit consultation and we will help you work out where to start.

Markdown Content:
Check out the Build Series. **[Part 1](https://promptledproduct.substack.com/p/i-broke-my-own-system-my-year-of) | [Part 2](https://promptledproduct.substack.com/p/how-i-built-a-self-correcting-data) | [Part 3](https://promptledproduct.substack.com/p/how-i-stopped-building-a-website) | [Part 4](https://promptledproduct.substack.com/p/lovable-just-launched-payments-here) | [Part 5](https://promptledproduct.substack.com/p/how-i-keep-my-ai-product-profitable)**

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-EnB!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F05708054-79b3-42ad-95a2-068d2f361475_1376x768.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-EnB!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F05708054-79b3-42ad-95a2-068d2f361475_1376x768.jpeg)

Every creator on [DraftKit](http://draftkit.app/) gets a public booking page at `draftkit.app/[their-username]`. No login required. Anyone can browse to it, fill out a collaboration request form, and the submission lands directly in that creator’s queue.

My own booking page is a good example. Take a look at it: **[https://draftkit.app/elenacalvillo](https://draftkit.app/elenacalvillo)**

That is the product. The problem is that bots do not write newsletters.

Three weeks after launching the public booking pages, a creator messaged me asking why her Collabs tab had 2 pending requests from names she didn’t recognize, with newsletter URLs that returned 404s. I pulled the `collab_requests` rows and found the pattern immediately: six from addresses ending in `.ru`, four with placeholder text in the message field, one that used `test123` as the Substack URL. None of them had triggered the SMART Match AI step, which was the tell. The bot had skipped the JavaScript-heavy portion of the form.

That same week I checked two other active booking pages for testing. One had 2 suspicious submissions, one had 1. I had shipped a public form with zero bot protection, and it took a creator complaint to find out.

If you have a public-facing form in your product, and especially if you built it with Lovable or a similar AI builder, you have likely shipped the same gap. AI builders scaffold the happy path. They do not add bot protection because they do not know your form will be indexed by every spam crawler running in 2026.

If you want someone to review where your public endpoints are exposed before a user notices, reach out at [hello@elenacalvillo.com](mailto:hello@elenacalvillo.com). Finding open insert paths on public tables is the first thing I check in a product audit.

[Cloudflare’s Radar data from 2025](https://blog.cloudflare.com/radar-2025-year-in-review/) showed bots generating the majority of HTML web traffic across their network, and the share has grown every quarter since. That measurement covers HTML requests: pages, forms, APIs. For publicly indexed booking forms that accept a name, an email, and a message with no authentication gate, the exposure is direct.

The SaaS products I audit are handling this in exactly two ways. Either they added bot protection before launch (rare), or they added it after the first creator or customer complaint (almost always). The cleanup cost is the same either way, but the trust damage only happens in the second scenario.

✅ Adding Turnstile before launch takes 30 minutes and costs nothing below one million monthly requests.

✅ Adding it after a creator goes public about spam in their queue takes longer and costs more than the dev time.

✅ The verification step that actually matters is server-side, not client-side. Most first implementations miss this.

The pattern is predictable. The form is scaffolded by an AI builder, which produces a React component that submits correctly, validates the email format, and inserts a row. Bot protection is not part of the happy path. The form goes live. It gets indexed. The spam arrives.

The window is not a failure of the AI builder. The threat model belongs to the product builder, and it was mine to add before launch.

When you build with Lovable, the AI generates the booking form, the submission handler, and the database insert. What it does not generate is the server-side step that confirms the submission came from a real browser rather than a script. Knowing that a form is public is not the same as modeling the downstream risk of that exposure.

The result is a functional product that passes every test you ran during development and then receives its first bot submission 72 hours after the domain goes live.

[Share](https://promptledproduct.substack.com/p/your-public-booking-form-is-a-bot?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

✅ **Add Cloudflare Turnstile to every public form before launch.** Turnstile is free up to one million requests monthly, invisible to real users, and requires only a script tag and a hidden response field in the form. It is the lowest-friction bot protection available in a Lovable-built product without a third-party subscription.

✅ **Verify the token server-side, in the edge function, before every database insert.** A client-side Turnstile check is bypassed by any bot that generates a valid-looking token string. The verification must happen in your Supabase edge function against Cloudflare’s `siteverify` endpoint. This is the step most first implementations skip, and it is the only step that actually confirms the token is real.

✅ **Add a second validation layer at the database level.** Triggers run regardless of how a row arrives, including direct API calls that bypass your edge function entirely. DraftKit’s `validate_requester_substack_url()` trigger rejects any submission with a non-publication URL. It is the last line of defense before any spam reaches the host’s queue.

✅ **Log every failed bot check.** When a Turnstile verification fails, write a row to your `analytics_events` table with the IP, timestamp, and which booking page was targeted. You want this data when a bot campaign targets a specific creator.

✅ **Audit every public endpoint before launch.** List every route that does not require authentication. For each one, ask whether it accepts user input that lands in your database. If yes, Turnstile goes on it before the domain is live.

If you want me to walk through your public endpoint map before the next feature ships, reach out at [hello@elenacalvillo.com](mailto:hello@elenacalvillo.com).

kept.heading: TIKTOK JUST MADE PAID SOCIAL AGENTIC (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: TikTok's new agentic AI tools can automate paid social execution, but the bigger shift is teaching AI how your team works. TikTok Ads MCP connects AI to campaign data and workflows, while Agentic Hub and Skills can package processes like creative fatigue analysis, budget optimization, reporting, and QA. Automate repeatable work, but keep humans involved in strategic decisions.
kept.article_text:
Title: TikTok Just Made Paid Social Agentic

URL Source: https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/tiktok-ads-mcp-agentic-ai-paid-social/

Published Time: 2026-09-01T15:19:42+00:00

Markdown Content:
TikTok is the latest platform to bring agentic AI directly into advertising workflows with the launch of [**TikTok Ads MCP and Agentic Hub**](https://ads.tiktok.com/business/en-US/blog/tiktok-agentic-hub-ai-agents-skills-mcp). And while the [MCP connector](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d9Q5r11fdns&pp=0gcJCRoMAYcqIYzv) itself is important, the more interesting development might be what TikTok is building on top of it.

Through TikTok Ads MCP, AI tools can connect directly to TikTok Ads to analyze performance, manage campaigns, work with audiences and creative, and execute advertising workflows without requiring marketers to move between their AI environment and Ads Manager. That direction should sound familiar. Meta recently introduced a similar model with its [Ads AI Connectors](https://www.facebook.com/business/news/meta-ads-ai-connectors). But TikTok is taking the concept a step further with Agentic Hub and Skills, creating an ecosystem where specific paid social workflows can essentially be packaged, reused, and shared.

That has much bigger implications than making campaign management faster. We’re starting to move toward a world where teams can encode how their best paid social practitioners actually work.

## **What TikTok Is Actually Building**

The MCP connector is the infrastructure layer. It gives AI agents access to TikTok Ads and allows them to interact with the platform through natural language.

Agentic Hub is where that access becomes more interesting. Instead of every marketer building prompts and workflows from scratch, TikTok Skills can package instructions, methodologies and processes around specific advertising tasks, then make those workflows available within supported AI environments.

Take creative fatigue. Today, a paid social practitioner might pull performance data, compare creatives, identify declining engagement or conversion efficiency, determine which assets are losing momentum, and recommend what should be refreshed.

A Skill can turn much of that methodology into a repeatable workflow. TikTok already has Skills designed to analyze creative fatigue and categorize ads based on whether they should be scaled, watched or retired. The same concept can extend to budget optimization, audience discovery, reporting, campaign QA and countless other workflows.

That also raises an important question about how much authority we give those workflows. Identifying creative fatigue is very different from automatically pausing the creative. Flagging inefficient spend is different from moving budget. As teams start encoding more of their methodology, they’ll also need to define what AI can act on independently, what requires approval and what should remain a human decision.

That changes the conversation around AI in paid social.

## **Where Human Judgment Still Has to Do the Work**

That doesn’t mean every workflow should be handed over to an agent. The useful distinction is **where repeatable logic ends and business judgment begins.** For teams starting to experiment with agentic paid social, I’d focus on four principles:

1.   **Start with repeatable workflows where the rules are clear.** Reporting, pacing checks, QA, creative fatigue monitoring and anomaly detection are natural starting points because they consume significant practitioner time without necessarily requiring a strategic decision at every step.
2.   **Encode your methodology, not just the task.** Asking an agent to “analyze this campaign” isn’t particularly differentiated. Defining exactly how your brand evaluates performance, which signals matter, what thresholds trigger concern, and how those signals translate into recommendations is where proprietary value starts to emerge.
3.   **Keep humans at the decision points that matter.** An agent can identify that creative performance is deteriorating or that one ad group is outperforming another. Deciding _why_, what that means for the broader strategy, and whether the business should respond still requires context the platform may not have.
4.   **Use the time saved to raise the bar for strategy.** If practitioners spend less time pulling reports, checking pacing and navigating campaign interfaces, the expectation shouldn’t simply become “do more campaigns.” That capacity should move toward creative strategy, experimentation, client consultation and connecting media performance to actual business outcomes.

There is another implication here that performance marketing leaders should be paying attention to. As platforms expose more of their advertising infrastructure to AI agents, platform execution becomes easier to replicate.

Knowing how to operate TikTok Ads Manager will still matter, but the advantage increasingly comes from knowing what an agent should do, when it should do it, what data it should consider, what guardrails it should follow and when its recommendation is wrong.

That puts more value on strategic judgment and systems thinking. For brands, it also creates an opportunity to turn years of accumulated expertise into infrastructure: taking the frameworks and decision-making processes that already drive performance and building them directly into how the team operates.

The competitive advantage isn’t simply access to the agent. Everyone will eventually have that. The advantage is what you teach the agent to do.

## **Bottom Line**

TikTok Ads MCP gives AI direct access to advertising workflows. Agentic Hub introduces something potentially more consequential: a way to make the methodologies behind those workflows reusable.

That points toward a different operating model for paid social teams. As more execution becomes agentic, teams will need to get much more deliberate about defining how they analyze performance, make decisions and govern what AI can act on.

The teams that get ahead will be the ones that can identify their strongest thinking, turn it into repeatable systems and use the capacity they create to make better strategic decisions.

Paid social expertise is becoming something teams can build into the system itself.

kept.article_text:
Title: Performance unlocked: Reddit Max campaigns are now available to all advertisers

URL Source: https://redditinc.com/news/performance-unlocked-reddit-max-campaigns-are-now-available-to-all-advertisers

Published Time: 2026-09-03T13:00:03.000Z

Markdown Content:
With more than 26 billion conversations on our platform, Reddit provides advertisers with a uniquely powerful source of real-time human insight and has become a proven performance driver for advertisers. Reddit delivers 2.1x higher incremental ROAS than the digital media average.

[Max campaigns](https://www.business.reddit.com/advertise/max-campaigns), in particular, have unlocked performance for advertisers of all sizes. Launched earlier this year in beta, Max campaigns automate targeting, creative selection and rotation, placements and budget allocation, while still providing advertisers with the right amount of control to apply their own strategic expertise. The results from early testing: advertisers see 17% lower costs/CPA and over 27% more conversions with Max campaigns.

What’s new with Max campaigns

Today, we are making Max campaigns available to all advertisers on Reddit and announcing three major updates to ensure they get even more value out of Max campaigns:

*   Advertising API Availability:R eddit’s A dvertising API now supports Max campaigns, enabling advertisers to create and manage them through supported third-party tools and workflows.

*   Smartly integration:Smartly is the [first third-party partner](https://www.smartly.io/resources/smartly-and-reddits-max-campaigns?utm_campaign=reddit-max&utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=social)to support Max campaigns, allowing advertisers to create, scale, and manage them directly through Smartly.
*   Asset groups: We are introducing asset groups, which allow advertisers to organize multiple sets of creative within a single Max campaign. Each asset group can represent a different product line or use case (ie: running shoes, training apparel, fitness accessories), and include its own headlines, media, and destination URL. Advertisers can also report on each group separately to understand which products and messages are driving performance.

_“Advertisers need confidence that their budgets are driving the outcomes that matter most to their business,” said Jyoti Vaidee, VP of Ads Product, Reddit. “Our goal is to give them the intelligence and automation to work more efficiently while keeping them in control, so they can move faster, make smarter decisions, and get more value from their investment.”_

![Image 1: max gtm gif](https://redditinc.com/hs-fs/hubfs/max%20gtm%20gif.gif)

How advertisers are putting Max campaigns to work

Advertisers are already using Max campaigns to turn automation into measurable momentum. Musical instrument manufacturer Fender leaned into Max campaigns during Black Friday shopping to reach new customers and drive efficient traffic to its site. Working with Gupta Media, Fender used a mix of banners, artist imagery, product shots, and video, while Max campaign’s AI helped match creative formats and messaging with relevant communities. The campaign delivered 148% ROAS, with CTR 126% higher than benchmark and CPC 46% more efficient than a standard campaign.

LensDirect used Max campaigns as part of an evergreen strategy to expand its reach, connect with new communities, and improve campaign efficiency. The contact lens retailer combined automatic targeting and retargeting with Max campaign’s ability to rotate headlines, images, and CTAs, allowing the campaign to serve the creative combination predicted to have the greatest impact without manual setup. LensDirect reported 5.5x overall ROAS and planned to continue scaling its presence on Reddit.

Title: Glossier and Dishoom’s Roya Shariat on building brands, following your curiosity, and designing an unconventional career

URL Source: https://embeddedbrandstrategy.substack.com/p/glossier-and-dishooms-roya-shariat

Published Time: 2026-09-04T13:32:48+00:00

Markdown Content:
Roya Shariat has the kind of career that any brand marketer would envy. She joined **Glossier** in 2018 after running into founder Emily Weiss on the street and pitching her on a role. After 6.5 years at Glossier, Roya moved to London, where she led brand and communications at cult restaurant chain **Dishoom**. In between, she also consulted with brands like **Ultra Violette** and the **Women’s Tennis Association Foundation.**

She is also really stylish, funny, and did I mention she is a [cookbook author](https://amzn.to/4gBP9tH) with her mom?

I caught up with her in London (over our favorite breakfast at Dishoom of course!) and asked her if she’d come on Brand Confessional to talk about how she has navigated building her career.

Check out the interview below, and her Substack, [Consumed](https://royas.substack.com/).

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!D1JT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fefc9e08d-8ab3-4e3a-9ccb-6999a305e945_2550x2072.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!D1JT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fefc9e08d-8ab3-4e3a-9ccb-6999a305e945_2550x2072.jpeg)

Roya Shariat

**Tell me about yourself: what do you do, and what’s the unfair advantage you bring to it?**

> I am a writer, and more broadly: a communicator. I like to take a dozen disparate threads and turn them into one cohesive story.
> 
> 
> I think what makes me good at this is a relentless curiosity. I treat my job like an investigative journalist and I think that’s how I’m able to get a pithy story out of it.

**Pitching is a big part of being a journalist. You ran into Glossier founder Emily Weiss on the street and pitched her on creating a social impact role. Why did you believe social impact was the next move for the cosmetics brand?**

> Glossier had an inherent ethos: to create the beauty products that people wanted to see in the world. Instead of deciding what to create and then pushing that on consumers, they were finding out what people wanted, often by interacting with customers directly via Glossier’s blog _Into the Gloss._
> 
> 
> This democratic approach resonated, but customers (myself included) wanted to know what the brand stood for beyond its products.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7GSw!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F11969cdd-95c1-4718-abc7-00f3a86657b7_1200x675.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7GSw!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F11969cdd-95c1-4718-abc7-00f3a86657b7_1200x675.png)

Glossier’s first [products](https://glossier.com/products/balm-dotcom) were inspired from customer feedback

**How did you pitch yourself for the role?**

> I showed up to the follow-up conversation with a five-slide presentation (printed out in Glossier font, in a pink pouch) about me, this potential role, and why _now_. One of those slides was filled with stats about how consumers are increasingly value-led in their purchasing choices, how team members want to work for companies that have a POV on impact, and so on.
> 
> 
> This deck accomplished two things. One, the stats showed why impact mattered, but, two, the team’s response to those stats told me if leadership would be genuinely bought into social impact work and take a long view.

**That’s an incredible story on how to create a job but also ensure the company is a fit for you.**

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zKAs!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd7d83b79-f0a5-49b4-ab6c-f1a8d3939453_2048x771.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zKAs!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd7d83b79-f0a5-49b4-ab6c-f1a8d3939453_2048x771.png)

**You then moved to Dishoom, one of London’s most beloved restaurants. How does working in brand at a service business differ from brand in a product company?**

> The channels are different. In a product business, your surfaces are communications and the product itself. In hospitality, the product is the _experience_. It’s the room, the hospitality, how you make someone feel when they are with you.
> 
> 
> What that means is you need to bring your hospitality team along for the ride. They are the ones delivering your brand. Think of them as your first customer. If they aren’t fully aware, excited, and supportive of what the brand is doing, you need to rethink it.

**Dishoom has expanded across the UK and will soon launch in New York City. Despite this, every location feels as authentic and true to Dishoom as the first. How does Dishoom maintain the potency of the brand while expanding?**

> Dishoom’s brilliant co-founder Shamil might be the one who coined the phrase “deepen, don’t dilute” (more from him on that [here](https://www.dishoom.com/journal/stories/goodbye-2024-hello-2025/)). Our co-founders have never wanted growth to dilute the quality of our food, or the happiness of our team and guests.

One lesson we learned was that whilst we were clearly running a business, elevating profit to the key focus wasn’t serving us. Instead we formulated a principle: ‘obsess over awesome food and drink, awesome service and a happy team, and control the costs. Then, revenue and profit are the applause that follow.

Dishoom founder Shamil Thakrar

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Q6kA!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa75ff8b2-13fb-4b6d-bade-1620dce580e3_1200x801.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Q6kA!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa75ff8b2-13fb-4b6d-bade-1620dce580e3_1200x801.png)

_Dishoom’s famous bacon naan roll_

**You’ve had a front row seat to two incredible brand founders in Emily Weiss and Shamil Thakrar. What did each teach you?**

> From Emily, I learned what devotion to the customer looks like, which entails a deep desire to learn more about them, to find opportunities to connect with them online and in person, and a relentless desire to improve their experience. Glossier was inherently curious, trying to understand routines and what might’ve been missing or what could’ve been better.
> 
> 
> From Shamil, there’s a dazzling quote from his late father that has become a core part of the Dishoom ethos: “For something to truly succeed, it must have a little poetry at the heart of it.” You can see that poetry (and that heart!) in so many ways, big and small, across Dishoom.

**Keep learning about your customer, and maintain the magic - great tips for those trying to scale a brand concept.**

**Speaking of brand builders, y ou’re also a builder yourself - you and your mom built a [cookbook brand](https://amzn.to/4gBP9tH) and a community of more than 200K across Instagram and TikTok.**

**How did you build Maman and Me?**

> Honestly, very scrappily! There was no strategy, never a content calendar, never even a regular cadence of posting. If something came to mind, it went out the door. This is absolutely terrible guidance for anyone doing this, because if I had more time and could approach this with more strategy and rigor, it could’ve been even bigger or could be a proper income-generating channel. But for me, it is a passion project.

[![Image 5: Maman and Me](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IJDk!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F812c2def-b4e0-4b32-9cc3-fd3e294d4adc_768x959.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IJDk!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F812c2def-b4e0-4b32-9cc3-fd3e294d4adc_768x959.jpeg)

[Maman & Me](https://amzn.to/4d1qT1P), a cookbook by Roya and her mother Gita

**That’s funny, because as an outsider it looks super professional.**

> When it comes to this kind of thing, my advice is: just try. Do not be afraid of being perceived or what others will think, do not let analysis paralysis stop you. Even the scrappy, imperfect version of your work can find resonance.

**What advice do you have for someone trying to break into brand marketing?**

> Talk to as many people as you possibly can, think of it as maximizing your surface area for luck (I did not coin that term, I read about it [here](https://usefulfictions.substack.com/p/how-to-increase-your-surface-area)). It is truly the loose ties - people you meet once or twice - who end up having more of a sway in your career than your managers or close teammates (I also didn’t make this up!).
> 
> 
> It’s a tenet of Meg Jay’s _[The Defining Decade](https://amzn.to/4zWzUmE),_ which I read once in my twenties and still lingers in my head.

**How about once you are in the interview process?**

> This might be corny, but showing up as my authentic self has helped a ton.
> 
> 
> My first boss at the Rockefeller Foundation asked me “What’s something not on your resume that you’re proud of?” in my job interview. I talked about my immigrant parents and the hustle they instilled in me, and my passion for food.
> 
> 
> At Glossier, my deep interest in beauty came through in the interviews, and in that pitch deck there was an “About Me” slide that mentioned I was reading one book a week for the past year and a half.
> 
> 
> At Dishoom, my [cookbook](https://amzn.to/4gBP9tH) - relegated to a line at the bottom of my resume! - was a real topic of conversation.

**I like that, it sounds like you’re saying, don’t forget to brand yourself and show up in a way that’s memorable and distinctive.**

> Yes!The right team will value your interests, your nerdiness, and anything cross-disciplinary you can bring to the table.

**Let’s close by looking towards the future. Which brand do you look at today and think, they are doing incredible work and will be the big brands of tomorrow?**

> I’m a big fan of [Bandit Running](https://embeddedbrandstrategy.substack.com/p/diary-of-a-brand-bandit-running). I lived in Greenpoint for a long time, where they’re based, and saw their business grow from scrappy challenger to a real contender in the running space. And [their shorts](https://go.shopmy.us/p-83972532) are my favorite. I LOVE that they support [unsponsored athletes](https://www.instagram.com/p/DbTNaFxlAkd/?hl=en&img_index=1) with unbranded kits, cash, and a contract that isn’t restricted (a beautiful way to weave impact into the brand).
> 
> 
> In the UK, [Perfumer H](https://www.instagram.com/perfumerhlondon/?hl=en) is incredibly curated and chic, with perfumes, incense and teas that are otherworldly. There’s an element of mystery and intrigue about the brand that draws you in.

**That’s funny you mention Bandit Running, because they’re one of my picks as well (and featured in [Diary of a Brand](https://embeddedbrandstrategy.substack.com/p/diary-of-a-brand-bandit-running)!).**

What I took away from our conversation is that building a career in brand takes creativity and smarts, but also the confidence to just try things. Roya had the confidence to pitch Emily Weiss, paired with the smart framing to show what impact could do for Glossier. She brought that same spirit to launching a cooking channel with her mom — and turned it into a brand of its own.

I’ve seen that “just do things” mentality work out in my own career, and this interview was a polite reminder to keep doing that.

As for what’s next for Roya? I’m not allowed to say. But I have a feeling you’ll want to keep an eye on her LinkedIn.

If you enjoyed this conversation, subscribe for more conversations with the people shaping how brands are built. And DM if you know a person or brand who would make a good feature.
